e-16522.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Matrix
e-16522.problem:
Let $J_n\left(\lambda\right)$ denote the $n \times n$ Jordan block matrix with $\lambda$ on the main diagonal. Then,  find
$e^{2\left(J_2(1) {\textstyle\:\oplus\:} J_2(3)\right)}.$
e-16522.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block $J_n(\lambda),$ we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/11519fece8adb61a999a33d66d9d61e3052709066702f96b8141a4574a8d86b8.png)

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2({J}_{2}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(3))} & ={e}^{2([\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(1) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{2}(3)\end{aligned}])} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2({J}_{2}(1))} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{2({J}_{2}(3))}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{2({J}_{2}(1))}\,⊕\,{e}^{2({J}_{2}(3))}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For $J_2(1),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda=1.$ Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{2x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(1)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2\cdot 1} & 2{e}^{2\cdot 1} \\ 0 & {e}^{2\cdot 1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2} & 2{e}^{2} \\ 0 & {e}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For $J_2(3),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda=3.$ Since $n=2,$ we need the first derivative of $f$ only, which we have already computed. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(3)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2\cdot 3} & 2{e}^{2\cdot 3} \\ 0 & {e}^{2\cdot 3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6} & 2{e}^{6} \\ 0 & {e}^{6}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/17b4d68be43e4a4eb895ebbe623b713f1a808153424dd221b7497579d666b00a.png)

Given that $V = PJP^{-1},$ find $\sin\left(\pi V\right).$
e-16517.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SAS^{-1}) = S \cdot f(A) \cdot S^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x) = \sin(\pi x)$ and the given matrix $V,$ we have

$$
\sin(\pi V) = \sin\left(\pi{PJP^{-1}}\right) = P \cdot (\sin(\pi J)) \cdot P^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $-3$s on the main diagonal, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/a8ad3d4a15a5a8e7307fdd6449d8086d6c9c7e656caea877d41f021c7d8584cc.png)

The derivative of $f$ is $f'(x) = \pi \cos \pi x.$ So, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/9af57a3b00b9c9e64508c119ae77690904bdb8c30b124b8165d4280149361bad.png)

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/ff9333784a9cdd38f510398b48e485764eac400f56c2cc9f2f1a18e5138845d8.png)

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi V) & =P\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi J))\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -\pi  \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\pi  & -\pi  \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\pi  & -\pi  \\ \pi  & -\pi \end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 4 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $M=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{ln}⁡M.$
after.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and the given matrix $M,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡M=\operatorname{ln}⁡(PJ{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡J)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $1$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡J=[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{x}.$ So, we get

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡J=[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) & \frac{1}{(1)} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2\cdot 2-3\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡M & =P\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡J)\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 4 \\ -9 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

content.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 4 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $M=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{ln}⁡M.$
content.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and the given matrix $M,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡M=\operatorname{ln}⁡(PJ{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡J)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $1$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡J=[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{x}.$ So, we get

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡J=[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) & \frac{1}{(1)} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2\cdot 2-3\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡M & =P\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡J)\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 4 \\ -9 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
K=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 6\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $K=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find ${3}^{K/2}.$
after.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)={3}^{x/2}$ and the given matrix $K,$ we have

$$
{3}^{K/2}={3}^{\frac{1}{2}PJ{P}^{-1}}=P\cdot ({3}^{J/2})\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $4$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=[\begin{aligned}f(4) & {f}^{′}(4) \\ 0 & f(4)\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{{3}^{x/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{2}.$ So, we get

$$
{3}^{J/2}=[\begin{aligned}f(4) & {f}^{′}(4) \\ 0 & f(4)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & \frac{9\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{2} \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$

content.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Decomposition
content.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
K=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 6\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $K=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find ${3}^{K/2}.$
content.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)={3}^{x/2}$ and the given matrix $K,$ we have

$$
{3}^{K/2}={3}^{\frac{1}{2}PJ{P}^{-1}}=P\cdot ({3}^{J/2})\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $4$s on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=[\begin{aligned}f(4) & {f}^{′}(4) \\ 0 & f(4)\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{{3}^{x/2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{2}.$ So, we get

$$
{3}^{J/2}=[\begin{aligned}f(4) & {f}^{′}(4) \\ 0 & f(4)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & \frac{9\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{2} \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{K/2} & =P\cdot ({3}^{J/2})\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & \frac{9\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{2} \\ 0 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}18-9\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & 9\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-9 \\ -18 & 18\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9-9\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & 9\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ -9\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & 9+9\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}\pi  & 2\pi  \\ 0 & 2\pi \end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}\pi  & 0 \\ 0 & 2\pi \end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $C=PD{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{cos}⁡C.$
after.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡C$ and the given matrix $C,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡C=\operatorname{cos}⁡(PD{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡D=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi \end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-2\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$

$$

content.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}\pi  & 2\pi  \\ 0 & 2\pi \end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}\pi  & 0 \\ 0 & 2\pi \end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $C=PD{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{cos}⁡C.$
content.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡C$ and the given matrix $C,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡C=\operatorname{cos}⁡(PD{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡D=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi \end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-2\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡C & =P\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
G=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}+2 & \,\,-2 \\ 2 & \,\,\sqrt{3}-2\end{aligned}],\,\,\,J=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & \,1 \\ 0 & \,\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}],\,\,\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $G=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find $12\operatorname{arctan}⁡G.$
after.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=12\operatorname{arctan}⁡x$ and the given matrix $G,$ we have

$$
12\operatorname{arctan}⁡G=12\operatorname{arctan}⁡(PJ{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (12\operatorname{arctan}⁡J)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $\sqrt{3}$ on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=[\begin{aligned}f(\sqrt{3}) & {f}^{′}(\sqrt{3}) \\ 0 & f(\sqrt{3})\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{12}{{x}^{2}+1}$ So, we get

$$
12\operatorname{arctan}⁡J=[\begin{aligned}f(\sqrt{3}) & {f}^{′}(\sqrt{3}) \\ 0 & f(\sqrt{3})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4\pi  & 3 \\ 0 & 4\pi \end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 2-2\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}12\operatorname{arctan}⁡G & =P\cdot (12\operatorname{arctan}⁡J)\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4\pi  & 3 \\ 0 & 4\pi \end{aligned}]\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2\pi +3 & 4\pi -3 \\ 4\pi  & -4\pi \end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\pi +6 & -6 \\ 6 & 4\pi -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
G=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}+2 & \,\,-2 \\ 2 & \,\,\sqrt{3}-2\end{aligned}],\,\,\,J=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & \,1 \\ 0 & \,\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}],\,\,\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $G=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find $12\operatorname{arctan}⁡G.$
content.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=12\operatorname{arctan}⁡x$ and the given matrix $G,$ we have

$$
12\operatorname{arctan}⁡G=12\operatorname{arctan}⁡(PJ{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (12\operatorname{arctan}⁡J)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $\sqrt{3}$ on the main diagonal, we have

$$
f(J)=[\begin{aligned}f(\sqrt{3}) & {f}^{′}(\sqrt{3}) \\ 0 & f(\sqrt{3})\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative of $f$ is ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{12}{{x}^{2}+1}$ So, we get

$$
12\operatorname{arctan}⁡J=[\begin{aligned}f(\sqrt{3}) & {f}^{′}(\sqrt{3}) \\ 0 & f(\sqrt{3})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4\pi  & 3 \\ 0 & 4\pi \end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 2-2\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}12\operatorname{arctan}⁡G & =P\cdot (12\operatorname{arctan}⁡J)\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4\pi  & 3 \\ 0 & 4\pi \end{aligned}]\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2\pi +3 & 4\pi -3 \\ 4\pi  & -4\pi \end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4\pi +6 & -6 \\ 6 & 4\pi -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
